Article Title: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei to AI companies: Fulfil your Cancer promise, rather than blaming me
Article Text:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei dismissed calls for AI firms to rely on glossy campaigns

A rare, lengthy social media post

What comes next, according to Dario Amodei

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has pushed back against criticism that warnings about AI risks are fuelling public negativity. In a post shared on social media platform X (formerly known as Twitter) Amodei said that the real issue is a ‘crisis of trust’ rooted in decades of suspicion toward companies, governments, and the tech industry. “Ordinary people don’t trust us and suspect we’re cooking up some new way to screw them over,” he wrote.Amodei dismissed calls for AI firms to rely on glossy campaigns to improve their image. “At this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliché than inspiring,” he said. Instead, he argued that the only way to rebuild trust is to actually deliver breakthroughs like curing cancer, rather than making promises that feel deceptive.Highlighting his own approach, Amodei said he is accountable to biomarkers and adjusts protocols based on measurable outcomes. He compared mastery in diet and health to excellence in academics, sports, or engineering, insisting that self‑control and discipline should be respected as legitimate forms of mastery.“I do agree that the public has a negative view of AI (and that this is a big problem), but I don’t think it is primarily caused by me or any other AI leader warning about AI’s risks.I think it is fundamentally a crisis of trust. I think that ordinary people don’t trust companies, governments, or the tech industry and always suspect that we are cooking up some new way to screw them over. The causes of this go back decades and AI is just the latest iteration of it. I don’t think that a glitzy marketing campaign with a positive spin (which some have advocated that Anthropic do) is the way to win back that trust — at this point, saying that AI will cure cancer is more a cliche than it is inspiring, and most people think it is deceptive. The thing that will work is *actually curing cancer*. I think by far the most accurate criticism of AI companies including Anthropic is that we haven’t yet delivered on our big promises to benefit the world. That is totally on us, and I think it’s the criticism you should be making, instead of all this stuff about messaging and marketing”, wrote Amodei on X.Amodei laid out his argument in an extended post on X on Saturday, a platform he generally avoids, according to a Fortune report. He began by addressing the debate around AI regulation, describing what he sees as a false choice between critics who worry regulation leads to concentrated corporate power and those who argue that widely distributing AI, including through open-weight models, is the better safeguard. Amodei argued that institutions like the court system show power can be decentralized without abandoning oversight, and noted that Anthropic has backed policies that would slow down frontier AI companies like itself while giving smaller competitors more room to operate.He acknowledged that AI does tend to concentrate power structurally, but attributed that tendency to the scaling laws underlying how AI models improve as more computing resources are put into them, rather than to regulation itself. In his view, open-weight models only shift that concentration toward whoever controls the most computing capacity and chips, rather than eliminating it. He said he favors "rules of the road" that address AI's cyber, biological and alignment risks while also institutionally constraining the power of frontier AI companies and leaving room for open-weight models, and voiced support for a FINRA-like regulatory body as well as the Trump administration's approach to AI testing.Amodei said Anthropic is trying to rebuild credibility by producing tangible results, pointing specifically to increased work in biology and medicine, and describing "early glimmers" of what he suggested could eventually be significant breakthroughs. Until there are actual accomplishments to point to, he said the company would avoid making further big promises and instead focus on being transparent about AI's risks in the meantime, arguing that honesty carries no more public credibility risk, and quite possibly less, than an approach that downplays or distracts from risks people already sense are real.
Article Summary: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has pushed back against criticism that warnings about AI risks are fuelling public negativity. ‘Ordinary people don’t trust us and suspect we’re cooking up some new way to screw them over,’ he wrote. He dismissed calls for AI firms to rely on glossy campaigns to improve their image.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Turning questions of identity into music, Juno-nominated Cheng² Duo comes to Pune
Article Text:
Cheng² Duo will perform at Mazda Hall on Tuesday, August 18, at 7 pm, in a concert organised by the Poona Music Society.

Pune:

TOI





Music, for siblings Bryan and Silvie Cheng, is as much about connection as about performance. The cello-piano duo’s band Cheng² Duo will perform in Pune on Tuesday, Aug 18, at a concert organised by the Poona Music Society at Mazda Hall, with works by Janáček, Nadia Boulanger, Poulenc and Mussorgsky.“This programme is an exploration of the full sound palette available to our instruments. Cello and piano have arguably the widest ranges of any duet combination, as we can go from the most intimate whisper to something almost symphonic in scope, and our own arrangement of Mussorgsky’s Pictures at an Exhibition leans into extended techniques to push that range even further,” Bryan toldEach work brings a different kind of storytelling — Janacek’s speech-inflected intensity, Boulanger’s harmonic sensitivity, Poulenc’s wit and lyricism and Mussorgsky’s vivid, almost theatrical imagery.Questions of identity and belonging have shaped their artistic journey all along. Album Portrait, which received a JUNO nomination, emerged during a period marked by a rise in anti-Asian racism and explored heritage through works by composers of Asian descent and arrangements of traditional Chinese music.Bryan says the making of Portrait swells them with pride. “What we’re most proud of is how accessible we’ve made its featured works, especially for the next generation of musicians.”They have self-published arrangements from the album, with digital scores purchased by musicians globally.“It brings us enormous joy and fulfillment to contribute to the growth of classical music, to broaden its embrace, and expand the curiosity of listeners and musicians alike,” he said.Bryan calls for classical music to better reflect the cultural and ethnic diversity of a modern globalised world. “It is so important for classical music to reflect the colourful fabric of society today. Historically, this art form’s canon has centred on figures from the European tradition, but we live in a global village, and there are so many fascinating voices from every kind of background who deserve to be heard. ”Their ‘pop hit’ arrangement of Horse Racing, which draws inspiration from a Chinese folk melody, has become their requested encore.They started playing music as children, and a lifetime of companionship has brought their musical and physical rhythms into sync, they say. That alone “gives us innate trust” and “a kind of telepathic, precognitive listening”.Every concert, Bryan says, gives them the thrill of interacting intimately with people through music in an otherwise superficial time.Making classical music accessible remains central to their work. “Ideally, even someone who’s never been to a classical concert or heard classical music at all ends up moved, discovering something new. Come with open ears and an open heart, and leave the rest to us,” he said.
Article Summary: The cello-piano duo’s band Cheng² Duo will perform in Pune on Tuesday, Aug 18, at a concert organised by the Poona Music Society. They will perform works by Janáček, Nadia Boulanger, Poulenc and Mussorgsky.

Article Title: ‘Robot boys’ steal show at Kavundampalayam govt School’s Independence Day event
Article Text: COIMBATORE: Students dressed up like robots stole the show at Independence Day celebrations at Kavundampalayam Government Higher Secondary School on Saturday.The school marked the 80th Independence Day with a blend of patriotism and technology as students from its STEM (science, technology, engineering and mathematics) laboratory took part in the parade and flag-hoisting dressed up as “robot boys. ”The robot-themed presentation drew attention for its creative use of innovation and STEM concepts, earning appreciation from those present. Trainers from the iExplore Foundation guided and supported the students in executing the idea.The school launched the “Cyber Champions Ambassador Programme” to promote cyber safety, responsible digital behaviour and effective use of technology. Under the initiative, selected student leaders will be trained to spread awareness on digital safety, cyber hygiene and online threats and to mentor peers.The celebrations highlighted the school’s focus on STEM education, creativity and digital awareness, with coordinated efforts from the administration, teachers, iExplore Foundation trainers and students.
Article Summary: Students from Kavundampalayam Government Higher Secondary School dressed up as “robot boys’ ” The robot-themed presentation drew attention for its creative use of innovation and STEM concepts. The celebrations highlighted the school’s focus on STEM education, creativity and digital awareness.

Article Title: 'I don’t feel rooted here': Indian couple in Ireland to return to Pune after 11 years, citing AI pressure and job stress
Article Text:
NRI couple in Ireland for 11 years to move back to Pune and raise daughters with grandparents.

Spent 11 years in Ireland

'I don't feel rooted here'

Internet reacts

An Indian tech couple living in Ireland for more than a decade say they plan to move back to Pune by May next year, citing rising work pressure, concerns about artificial intelligence and the lack of family support while raising their two daughters.The couple shared their plans in a Reddit post, saying their children currently spend most of their day in childcare and school-related arrangements because the family has no relatives nearby.They said their routine in Ireland typically runs from 8am to 6pm, with the children moving between creche, breakfast club, school and after-school care while both parents work.“In Pune they walk out of school into their grandparents' home. This single picture does more work in my decision than any spreadsheet,” they wrote.The couple said returning to Pune would mean their daughters could spend more time with their grandparents, while the family would also have help with cooking and household chores.After 11 years in Ireland, the couple said they no longer wanted to manage work, childcare and household responsibilities without family support.They also said they were increasingly worried about the pressure created by technological and AI changes in the workplace.The couple argued that their parents' ability to spend time with their grandchildren is more valuable now than waiting another decade.“The grandparents' healthy years are now. Not in 10 years, when we'd return for hospital duty instead of daily life,” they wrote.They said their parents had previously visited Ireland for a month but found the experience difficult, making a permanent move there unrealistic.The couple also described a sense of detachment after spending more than a decade in Ireland.They said they had built a functional life there but still did not feel they had developed deep roots.“After 11 years I don't feel rooted here myself,” they said.They also described missing the everyday family and cultural connections they associate with India, arguing that celebrations and social life felt different when experienced away from their wider family.The couple said they had generally found Ireland more welcoming than the UK or US, but still felt that subtle experiences of being an outsider could affect children growing up there.Several users responded with their own experiences of living in Ireland.One user said they had moved to Ireland only recently with an infant but were already considering returning to India.“I'm in Ireland as well; I moved here recently(not even months) and am still feeling that I should move back to India. We moved here with our infant thinking it'll be better for her future, but considering the health and the daily hustle here, it feels like India would be better. She can decide for herself whether she wants to move back here or not, but we definitely are moving back within a year.”Another user said changing attitudes towards immigration could also influence people's decisions to remain in Ireland or Britain.“I would add one more reason to do so: Ireland and Britain are on a trajectory of becoming less and less welcoming to immigration. Ireland and especially the Britain that is now is not what it will be in 5 years.”A third user responded:“Wish you all the best! Good decision.”
Article Summary: Indian tech couple living in Ireland for more than a decade say they plan to move back to Pune. They cite rising work pressure, concerns about artificial intelligence and the lack of family support while raising their two daughters. The couple said returning to India would mean their daughters could spend more time with their grandparents.

Article Title: Archaeologists find earliest physical evidence of brass-making in East Asia in southern China
Article Text:
Archaeologists find the earliest physical evidence of brass-making in East Asia in southern China (PC: Cambridge University Press)

Ancient crucibles reveal early brass-making in medieval China

Ancient crucibles reveal early brass-making in medieval China (PC: AI Generated)

How did ancient craftspeople make brass from copper and zinc

How did brass-making technology reach medieval Guangzhou

What does the discovery reveal about medieval metallurgy in China

A set of ancient crucibles found in Guangzhou is giving archaeologists new clues about how brass-making technology may have reached medieval China. The vessels came from an official metallurgical workshop at the Royal Palace of the Nanyue Kingdom and dated from the ninth and tenth centuries AD. Their metal residues show that craftspeople were producing brass locally through cementation rather than simply working with imported objects. According to a research article published by Cambridge University Press, titled ‘ Brass technology transmission via maritime routes: crucible evidence from southern China ’, points towards wider technological connections with the Islamic world. Guangzhou was a major trading port, and the authors suggest maritime routes may have helped move metallurgical knowledge across regions. The study analysed crucibles using chemical, microscopic and lead-isotope methods. Together, the findings provide direct archaeological evidence for medieval brass production in southern China and offer clues about how the technology may have travelled.Archaeologists found three well-preserved brass-making crucibles at an official metallurgical workshop in Guangzhou. The workshop was part of the Royal Palace of the Nanyue Kingdom site and was active across many centuries.The three crucibles belong to the ninth–tenth century group. Each was cup-shaped with a slightly inward-sloping rim and a rounded base. Some had a pouring spout. They measured about 60-80 mm across and 60-70 mm high, with a capacity of roughly 0.2-0.3 litres. Researchers found heavy heat damage and glassy material on their surfaces. Metal residues inside included copper, zinc compounds and brass droplets. A nearby semi-subterranean furnace also dates to the seventh-tenth centuries. Together, these remains provide direct evidence of metalworking at the site.The crucial evidence came from residues left inside the crucibles. Microscopic and chemical analyses identified zinc oxide, zinc silicate, and droplets of brass. One group of crucibles contained high-purity copper and binary brass droplets with about 11-17% zinc. Another contained bronze with tin alongside zinc and produced a copper-zinc-tin alloy. The researchers interpret these residues as evidence for cementation. In this process, zinc-bearing material is heated with copper or a copper alloy so zinc enters the metal and forms brass. The remains therefore show more than the presence of finished brass objects. They preserve traces of the production process itself.The study also examined lead isotopes to investigate the likely origin of the raw materials. The three analysed crucibles had similar lead-isotope ratios that fit signatures associated with the Cathaysia tectonic province. Because these signatures occur widely across southern China, the researchers say a local source for the raw materials is reasonable. The technology itself may have travelled from farther west. The authors point to similarities between the Guangzhou crucibles and brass-making vessels associated with the Islamic world. Guangzhou was also a major international trading port. Historical evidence records connections between the city and Arab merchants. The researchers therefore suggest that maritime routes and the movement of merchants and craftsmen may have helped transmit brass-making knowledge to southern China.The findings add important evidence to the history of brass production in China. Local brass production is generally thought to have begun around the tenth century AD, but the Guangzhou crucibles provide direct evidence from the ninth-tenth centuries. The researchers argue that the discovery helps explain how a specialised metallurgical technique became established locally. It also shows why archaeological workshops can reveal details that written records alone cannot provide. The study does not claim that every element of brass technology came from one place or through one route. Instead, it highlights a possible connection between western technological traditions, maritime trade and local production in Guangzhou. The evidence adds an important piece to the history of metallurgy in East Asia.
Article Summary: Archaeologists found three well-preserved brass-making crucibles at an official metallurgical workshop in Guangzhou. The crucibles dated from the ninth and tenth centuries AD. Their metal residues show that craftspeople were producing brass locally through cementation rather than simply working with imported objects.

Article Title: In 1745, the US welcomed mimosa trees for their pink flowers; they later escaped gardens and spread as an invasive species
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How mimosa escaped gardens and spread as an invasive tree

Image AI generated

Mimosa tree seeds and seed pods help the invasive species spread

Where mimosa is invasive across the eastern and south-western US

Why mimosa is difficult to control as an invasive tree

Around 1745, mimosa arrived in the United States as an ornamental tree, prized for its fragrant pink flowers, delicate foliage and unusual habit of folding its leaves at night. What began as a garden favourite, however, did not stay neatly within gardens. Albizia julibrissin escaped cultivation and gradually established itself along roadsides, clearings, flood plains and other disturbed areas across parts of the southern and eastern US. Its ability to grow quickly, produce large numbers of seeds and resprout after being cut has helped it persist and spread, while its seed pods can be moved by wind and water. In areas where mimosa forms dense stands, it can compete with native trees and shrubs and alter habitat along forest edges and waterways. The tree is now considered invasive in parts of the south-east, turning a once-popular ornamental into a persistent landscape management problem.Its spread also highlights how seemingly harmless landscaping choices can introduce species that later become difficult to control, especially in warm climates where mimosa can thrive and reproduce rapidly.Mimosa is native to southern Asia, with its natural range extending from Iran to Japan.Its arrival in the United States in 1745 was tied to its use as an ornamental rather than as a forestry or agricultural crop. The attraction was easy to understand. The tree produces fragrant pink flowers during the warmer months, with each flower cluster resembling a small powder puff. Its foliage is just as distinctive: long stems carry numerous tiny leaflets, creating the feathery appearance associated with the species. The leaves also fold down at night and can close in response to touch, adding to its unusual character.That combination of flowers, fragrance and delicate foliage made mimosa suited to gardens, but its growth habits eventually became a problem outside them. The tree can grow rapidly and reach roughly 20 to 40 feet in height, with a broad crown that may spread 20 to 50 feet. It is also capable of tolerating different soil, moisture and light conditions. Such flexibility matters when a plant escapes cultivation. Instead of remaining restricted to carefully maintained garden beds, mimosa can establish in places where vegetation has been disturbed and where native plants are already competing for space.The tree's spread is closely linked to its ability to produce and disperse seeds. Mimosa develops long, flat seed pods, with each pod containing several seeds. The pods can remain attached to the tree into winter, while mature seeds are dispersed during the autumn months. Wind and water can carry them away from the parent tree, and animals may also contribute to their movement. This gives mimosa several routes into new areas rather than relying on one method of reproduction.There is another complication once the plant has established itself. Cutting a mimosa does not necessarily mean the tree has been eliminated. The species can resprout after being cut or damaged, while root cuttings can also produce new plants. The Maryland Invasive Species Council has described mimosa as capable of invading riparian areas, old fields and roadsides after escaping from cultivated landscapes. Its seeds can remain dormant for years because of their hard, impermeable coats, making established populations more difficult to remove completely.Mimosa is now found across parts of the eastern and south-western United States and is invasive in areas of the south-east. Its preferred habitats are not limited to forests. Roadsides, vacant lots, grasslands, clearings and floodplain areas can all provide opportunities for it to establish. In these settings, seedlings may develop into groups of trees rather than remaining as isolated garden specimens.As those trees grow, their canopies can alter conditions for plants beneath them. The Master Gardeners of Northern Virginia note that mimosa can form dense stands at forest edges, where it may displace native trees and shrubs. It can also spread along roadsides and vacant lots and degrade habitat around streams. Seed pods carried by waterways and drainage ditches can help move the plant beyond the original site, extending the problem from one garden or property to a much larger area.Mimosa combines several traits that make control more complicated than simply removing a visible tree. It produces large quantities of seed, can tolerate a range of growing conditions and can regenerate after cutting. As per The National Cooperative Extension, the species is aggressive, weedy and high-maintenance, while its average lifespan is about 30 years. Its branches are weak and brittle, leaving established trees vulnerable to damage from strong winds, snow and ice.Control therefore has to deal with both existing plants and the next generation. Young seedlings can be removed before they become established, while larger trees may require cutting followed by further treatment because of their tendency to resprout. The Maryland Invasive Species Council recommends preventing seed production where possible and describes mechanical removal, girdling and carefully applied herbicide treatments as possible control approaches. There are no known biological control agents for mimosa, according to the same source.Mimosa also brings less obvious problems for people who keep it around homes. The tree sheds leaves, flowers and seed pods, creating regular clean-up work, and its weak wood can make branches susceptible to breakage. North Carolina State University lists the species as invasive, messy, weedy and short-lived, and also records pests and diseases including mimosa webworms, mites, root rot and Fusarium wilt.The story of mimosa is therefore not really about a plant that suddenly became harmful. It is about what happened after a tree valued for its appearance was moved far beyond its original range. In gardens, its pink flowers and unusual foliage made it an attractive ornamental. Outside those controlled settings, the same plant could reproduce, spread and establish in places where it was not wanted. Today, extension services recommend native alternatives such as serviceberry, flowering dogwood and eastern redbud for landscapes where a similarly ornamental small tree is wanted.
Article Summary: Mimosa arrived in the United States in 1745 as an ornamental tree. It is now considered invasive in parts of the south-east of the country. Its ability to grow quickly, produce large numbers of seeds and resprout after being cut has helped it spread.

Article Title: Meet Ananya Nagendra, the 18-year-old Texas student who built an ant-based digester for landfill food waste; tests found her prototype was about 83% efficient
Article Text:
Ananya Nagendra, the 18-year-old Texas student (Image Credit: Society For Science)

The problem with food waste

Four ant species were tested

From experiment to prototype

Prototype showed 83% efficiency

A finalist at a major science competition

Turning a small insect into a big idea

Food waste is usually thought of as a problem that begins in the kitchen and ends in a garbage bin. But once that waste reaches a landfill, it can create another environmental problem: methane. Ananya Gulur Nagendra, an 18-year-old student from Plano, Texas, wondered whether one of nature’s smallest scavengers could help tackle some of that waste. For her Regeneron Science Talent Search project, she studied how ants could break down food waste and developed a prototype of an ant-based aerobic digester. Her experiments compared four ant species to determine which could consume the most waste. She found that Camponotus castaneus performed particularly well and used those findings to design her system. Tests of the prototype found it was about 83% efficient. According to the Society for Science, which featured Nagendra as a 2026 Regeneron Science Talent Search finalist, her research could point toward a new approach to reducing the environmental impact of food waste in landfills.Food waste does not simply disappear after it is thrown away. When large amounts of organic material are buried in landfills, it decomposes under conditions that can produce methane, a powerful greenhouse gas.According to the Society for Science, food waste produces about 58% of methane emissions from landfills. That makes finding ways to manage discarded food particularly important for efforts to reduce the environmental impact of waste. Instead of looking for an entirely artificial solution, Nagendra explored something that already exists in nature. Ants are natural scavengers and regularly collect and consume food materials. Her project examined whether their feeding behaviour could be used in a controlled system to help break down food waste.Nagendra began her research by testing four different species of ants. The aim was to determine how much food waste each species could break down per ant each day. The experiments showed that Camponotus castaneus consumed the greatest amount of food waste among the tested species. The species also had the highest metabolic rate, making it the strongest candidate for the system she was developing.This part of the research was important because the project was not simply based on the idea that ants eat food waste. Nagendra wanted measurable evidence showing which species could perform the task most effectively. By comparing the species, she could identify the ant that appeared most promising for a potential waste-processing system.After identifying C. castaneus as the most effective species in her tests, Nagendra took the project a step further. She developed a model to estimate how much methane emissions could potentially be reduced through the ants' activity. The model connected the amount of food waste consumed with the potential environmental benefit of diverting some of that waste from conventional landfill decomposition. She then designed a prototype of an ant-based aerobic digester specifically for food waste.An aerobic digester is designed to allow decomposition to occur in the presence of oxygen. In Nagendra's concept, ants become part of the biological process rather than relying entirely on conventional mechanical or chemical treatment methods.The proposed system was also designed with cost in mind. According to the Society for Science, Nagendra estimated that a larger version of the system could cost less than $50,000.The most notable result came when Nagendra tested her prototype. The system was found to be about 83% efficient, according to the Society for Science. That result suggests the concept was capable of processing a substantial portion of the food waste under the conditions tested.It is important to note that this was a student research prototype, rather than a commercially deployed landfill system. The finding therefore represents an early-stage demonstration of the concept rather than proof that ant-based digesters are ready to replace existing waste-management infrastructure. Still, the result provides a basis for further research. Additional work could examine how the system performs with different types and quantities of food waste, how the ants behave over longer periods and how the approach might work at a much larger scale.Nagendra's work earned her a place among the finalists of the 2026 Regeneron Science Talent Search, one of the country's major science competitions for high school students. The 2026 finalist group included students from 35 schools across 15 states. They were selected from 300 scholars and 2,612 entrants, with more than $1.8 million in prizes available, including a top prize of $250,000. As per The Society for Science, the finalists were chosen based on the originality and creativity of their research, as well as their achievements and leadership.Nagendra's project stands out because it connects a familiar environmental problem with an unconventional biological solution. Rather than treating ants simply as insects found around discarded food, her research asks whether their natural behaviour can become part of a controlled waste-management process.The idea behind Nagendra's project is relatively simple: if ants can naturally consume and break down food, perhaps their abilities can be harnessed to process some of the waste that would otherwise end up in landfills. Her research does not solve the food-waste problem on its own, but it demonstrates how biological processes can inspire new approaches to environmental challenges.For an 18-year-old student, developing the idea from species testing to mathematical modelling and finally to a working prototype represents a substantial research journey. And with an efficiency of about 83% in her tests, Nagendra's ant-based digester offers an intriguing starting point for researchers interested in finding more sustainable ways to deal with food waste.
Article Summary: Ananya Gulur Nagendra, an 18-year-old student from Plano, Texas, wondered whether one of nature’s smallest scavengers could help tackle some of that waste. Her experiments compared four ant species to determine which could consume the most waste. She found that Camponotus castaneus performed particularly well and used those findings to design her system. Tests of the prototype found it was about 83% efficient.

Article Title: Meet Vedika Devarajan, the Washington high-school freshman who designed a banana-inspired neonatal incubator liner to tackle hospital-acquired infections
Article Text:
Vedika Devarajan (Image Credit: Regeneron ISEF)

The problem she wanted to solve

Why a banana leaf?

How BananaBaby works

Designed with developing countries in mind

From Washington fair to global competition

A small idea inspired by nature

A hospital incubator is designed to give premature and vulnerable newborns a controlled environment where they can receive the care they need. But maintaining a clean environment around vulnerable newborns can be challenging, particularly in places where medical resources are limited. Vedika Devarajan, a freshman at Redmond High School in Washington, approached the problem from an unexpected direction: a banana leaf. Her project, called BananaBaby, uses the structure of Musa species leaves as inspiration for a biomimetic neonatal incubator liner designed to help prevent hospital-acquired infections. The project went on to compete at the 2026 Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF), where Devarajan received a third-place award of $1,200 in Materials Science. According to the International Science and Engineering Fair, her project explores a low-cost approach to improving neonatal incubator design, particularly for developing countries.Hospital-acquired infections, or HAIs, are infections that patients can develop while receiving medical care. For newborns, particularly premature babies, infections can be especially dangerous because their immune systems are still developing.Neonatal incubators help regulate conditions around vulnerable babies, but their internal surfaces can also become exposed to moisture. Condensation can create moisture on incubator surfaces, which may contribute to conditions that support microbial contamination.Devarajan's project focuses on the incubator liner rather than attempting to redesign the entire incubator. Her idea was to create a surface that could manage condensation more effectively and potentially reduce opportunities for contamination.The inspiration came from the structure of banana leaves. Banana leaves have distinctive veins that run through their surfaces. Their distinctive vein patterns influence how water moves across the leaf, inspiring Devarajan's design. Devarajan looked at this natural pattern and asked whether it could be recreated artificially for use inside a neonatal incubator.Her project is described as “Musa spp. anisotropic and parallel venation biomimetic neonatal incubator liner”. In simpler terms, she created a material inspired by the directional vein patterns found in banana leaves and investigated whether that structure could help redirect condensation. This approach exemplifies biomimicry, where scientists and engineers study structures found in nature and use them as inspiration for solving human problems.The project involved creating a mold based on the venation pattern of a Musa species leaf. According to the ISEF project description, Devarajan used a polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) mold to reproduce the leaf-inspired structure. The resulting liner is designed around the idea of directing condensation rather than simply allowing moisture to remain on a surface. That distinction is important. In a conventional flat surface, water can form droplets and remain in place. Devarajan's structured surface is intended to encourage condensation to move along specific pathways. By taking inspiration from the parallel veins of banana leaves, Devarajan's design attempts to give condensation a more controlled route.The goal is not simply to change the appearance of an incubator. Instead, the project aims to address condensation and explore whether a relatively low-cost liner could help reduce conditions associated with contamination.Another important part of the project is its intended application. The full project title specifically refers to preventing hospital-acquired infections in developing countries. This makes affordability and practicality particularly relevant.Advanced medical equipment can be expensive, and hospitals with limited resources may not always have access to the newest technologies. A liner that could be manufactured using relatively accessible materials and production techniques could potentially offer a more practical way to improve existing equipment.However, BananaBaby remains a student research project rather than a clinically approved medical product. Further testing would be needed before such a liner could be used routinely in hospitals, including studies involving real clinical environments and microorganisms.Devarajan's project first gained recognition at the Washington State Science & Engineering Fair, where she earned first place and qualified for the international competition. She was listed as a ninth-grade student from Redmond High School.She then took BananaBaby to the 2026 Regeneron ISEF in Phoenix, Arizona. More than 1,700 high-school researchers from more than 65 countries participated in the competition, according to Lake Washington School District.At ISEF, Devarajan earned a Third Award of $1,200 in Materials Science for project MATS063. She also received recognition through a Non-Trivial Fellowship Scholarship. The award recognised her project among the student research entries in the Materials Science category.What makes BananaBaby interesting is the simplicity of its starting point. Devarajan did not begin by trying to redesign an entire neonatal care system. Instead, she looked closely at something found in nature, a banana leaf, and considered whether its structure could offer an answer to a medical problem. Her project demonstrates how biomimicry can connect natural structures with practical engineering challenges. The banana leaf's veins became the inspiration for a liner designed to manage condensation inside neonatal incubators.For a high-school freshman, taking that idea from observation to an engineered prototype and then presenting it at one of the world's largest pre-college science competitions is a notable achievement. More importantly, BananaBaby shows how even a familiar object from everyday life can inspire a scientific question with potential relevance to healthcare.
Article Summary: Vedika Devarajan, a freshman at Redmond High School in Washington, used the structure of Musa species leaves as inspiration for her project. BananaBaby is a biomimetic neonatal incubator liner designed to help prevent hospital-acquired infections. The project went on to compete at the 2026 Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair (ISEF)

Article Title: Arizona man, 88, and his dog got stuck overnight in monsoon mud with no cell service; how one emergency SOS text helped save them
Article Text:
(Image Credit: Yavapai County Sheriff's Office via FOX 10 Phoenix)

Vehicle became stuck in mud

SOS message revealed his location

Rescue teams reached the pair

He stayed with his vehicle

A small phone feature made a big difference

An 88-year-old Arizona man and his dog spent an entire night stranded in a remote part of Yavapai County after their vehicle became stuck in thick mud following recent monsoon storms. The man had been travelling on a back route between Carefree and Bloody Basin when conditions became too difficult for his vehicle to continue. The area had little access to regular communication, but the driver was able to use an emergency SOS text feature on his phone. That message gave authorities the information they needed to locate him, even though there was no traditional cell service where he was stranded. Rescue teams eventually reached the man and his dog early Friday morning. Both were found safe and unharmed. According to FOX 10 Phoenix , the emergency SOS feature helped officials pinpoint the man's location.The incident happened Thursday after the 88-year-old man decided to take back roads while travelling between Carefree and Bloody Basin in Yavapai County.Recent monsoon storms had left the remote backcountry roads in extremely poor condition. The rain had turned parts of the route into thick, muddy terrain, making it difficult for vehicles to pass.At some point, the man's vehicle became stuck in the mud, leaving him and his dog stranded miles away from the main dirt road. Because the area was so remote, getting help was not as simple as making an ordinary phone call.According to the Yavapai County Sheriff's Office, there was no regular cell service available at the location. The man, however, was able to use his phone's emergency SOS text function.The emergency feature proved crucial because it allowed officials to receive his location despite the lack of normal cellular service. The SOS message provided authorities with his precise coordinates, giving rescuers a clear idea of where they needed to go. Without that location information, finding a stranded person in the vast and difficult backcountry could have taken considerably longer.FOX 10 Phoenix reported that Yavapai County Sheriff's Office Forest Patrol deputies received the urgent report and began coordinating the response. The rescue was complicated by the same muddy and waterlogged conditions that had trapped the man's vehicle in the first place. Crews had to navigate difficult terrain to reach him.Yavapai County Forest Patrol deputies were joined by members of the county's search-and-rescue team, 4x4 units and the Jeep Posse. Using the location information supplied through the emergency SOS message, the teams were able to make their way toward the stranded vehicle. The difficult terrain meant rescuers had to use vehicles capable of handling the muddy backcountry.They eventually reached the 88-year-old man and his dog early Friday morning. Both were found safe and unharmed. The man declined medical attention after being rescued, according to the Yavapai County Sheriff's Office.The successful rescue came after the pair had spent the entire night in the remote area.One of the most important decisions the man made after becoming stranded was to remain with his vehicle rather than attempt to walk through the unfamiliar backcountry.The sheriff's office also said he had been prepared with food, water and his necessary medications. Those supplies helped him get through the night while he waited for rescuers to arrive.In a statement following the rescue, the sheriff's office said that although travelling on remote, unpaved roads during recent monsoon storms was not advisable, the man did two important things correctly once the emergency occurred: he stayed with his vehicle and knew how to use the emergency SOS feature.The incident highlights how emergency satellite-based messaging can become especially important in remote areas where conventional cell service is unavailable.In this case, one SOS message gave rescuers the location information they needed to find an elderly man and his dog in difficult terrain after a night of severe weather. The rescue also serves as a reminder of the risks associated with travelling on unpaved backcountry roads during Arizona's monsoon season. Roads that may appear passable in dry weather can quickly become muddy, flooded or nearly impossible to cross after heavy storms.For the 88-year-old driver and his dog, however, knowing how to use the emergency feature, staying with the vehicle and having basic supplies on hand helped turn a potentially dangerous situation into a safe rescue.
Article Summary: 88-year-old Arizona man and his dog became stranded after their vehicle became stuck in thick mud following recent monsoon storms. The area had little access to regular communication, but the driver was able to use an emergency SOS text feature on his phone. That message gave authorities the information they needed to locate him, even though there was no traditional cell service where he was stranded. Rescue teams eventually reached the pair early Friday morning.

Article Title: Ferrari’s first all-electric car sells for $40 million at charity auction, nearly 40 times initial estimate of $1.1 million; buyer won’t receive it until 2027
Article Text:
Ferrari’s Luce “Chassis 0” sets a new auction record after selling for $40 million at charity auction.

Ferrari Luce breaks previous $26 million record

Ferrari Luce packs four electric motors, 1,050 cv of power, a 310 km/h top speed and a 530 km claimed range.

What makes the $40 million Ferrari Luce special?

With a 122 kWh battery, 800V architecture and 1,050 cv, Ferrari’s Luce accelerates from 0 to 100 km/h in just 2.5 seconds.

Ferrari Luce packs more than 1,000 horsepower

Ferrari’s Luce brings supercar performance to its first EV.

Ferrari aims to make its EV feel like a Ferrari

Ferrari’s first all-electric vehicle has made history even before reaching its buyer. A bespoke 2026 Ferrari Luce, identified as “Chassis 0” and described as the first production chassis from the Luce programme, sold for exactly $40 million at an RM Sotheby’s charity auction in Monterey on Saturday.As Road & Track reported, the record-breaking sale makes the electric Ferrari the most expensive new car ever sold at auction. The auction house waived its buyer’s premium, meaning the entire $40 million will go to The Ferrari Foundation, which plans to use the proceeds for future educational initiatives.Despite the eye-watering sale price, the buyer will not take delivery of the car until the first quarter of 2027. The vehicle is expected to return to Ferrari’s headquarters in Maranello before being delivered.The $40 million sale surpassed the previous record set in 2025, when a customised Ferrari Daytona SP3 sold for $26 million at auction.The Luce’s result is particularly notable given the criticism Ferrari faced from some traditionalists following the unveiling of its first fully electric model. Ferrari introduced the Luce in May with a starting price of €550,000, or around $636,356.The vehicle represents a major departure from Ferrari’s traditional combustion-engine sports cars. The model was designed in collaboration with LoveFrom, the design studio founded by former Apple design chief Jony Ive.The auction car was created through Ferrari’s Tailor Made programme and was designed around the theme of light. Its bespoke exterior is finished in Madreperla Semi-Gloss, featuring a dedicated pigment that shifts between green and violet depending on the angle and intensity of the light.Inside, the cabin is upholstered in Perla Le Mans metallic leather made from selected Swiss hides. Other interior elements that would typically be black have been finished in Grigio Corvara.The car also features bespoke wheels, customised brake calipers and a Ferrari logo set against an optical-white background. Ferrari says the complexity of the paint application means that no two examples will look exactly alike.However, the biggest distinction is its “Chassis 0” status. Ferrari describes it as the first production chassis of the Luce programme, giving the buyer a unique piece of the marque’s electric-car history.According to Ferrari’s official website, the Luce is powered by four electric motors, with one motor driving each wheel. The powertrain produces 1,050 cv and allows the car to accelerate from 0 to 100 km/h in 2.5 seconds.The electric four-door has a claimed top speed of 310 km/h and a range of 530 kilometres on a full charge. It uses a 122 kWh battery pack, an 800-volt electrical architecture and weighs 2,260 kilograms.Ferrari describes the Luce as a spacious hatchback capable of seating five people.The vehicle uses a new vehicle control unit designed to network its various systems, with targets updated 200 times per second. The front motors produce 210 kW at the axle, while the rear motors generate 620 kW.Ferrari has also focused heavily on preserving the driving character associated with its combustion-engine models.The Luce features a separate elastically mounted subframe, which Ferrari says is a first for the brand and helps reduce unwanted vibrations. A precision accelerometer at the centre of the rear axle monitors the natural frequencies of rotating components.Ferrari says those frequencies are then processed to create a sound reminiscent of the brand’s traditional engines, using an approach similar to that of an electric guitar.The car also features a Torque Shift Engagement system designed to progressively deliver torque during cornering. An e-manettino manages power, torque curves, traction and performance through Range, Tour and Performance settings.Ferrari CEO Benedetto Vigna said after the car’s unveiling that the Luce had attracted orders from both existing and new customers.“The Ferrari Luce has nothing to do with electric cars you have seen from other players,” Vigna said in May, adding that customers would need to see and drive the car to understand how distinct its design, performance and interior are.With its $40 million charity-auction sale, the Ferrari Luce has now secured a place in automotive history before its first customer delivery.
Article Summary: A bespoke 2026 Ferrari Luce sold for exactly $40 million at an RM Sotheby’s charity auction in Monterey on Saturday. The sale makes the electric Ferrari the most expensive new car ever sold at auction. Despite the eye-watering sale price, the buyer will not take delivery of the car until the first quarter of 2027.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:
Your credit score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity.

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
Article Summary: Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.

Article Title: Google rejigs AI leadership as DeepMind CEO shifts role
Article Text:

Google parent company Alphabet on Wednesday announced a leadership overhaul of its AI division, with AI chief Demis Hassabis leaving his main managerial role and as several leaders of its Gemini model, including veteran engineer Jeff Dean, left the company to launch a startup called Discovery Loop. Article Title: Apple left a video of its camera AirPods inside a Mac update, and this is what they look like
Article Text:
Apple demoed a camera you can't see, in a video it didn't mean to publish.

AirPods cameras are for Siri, not for you to click photos

A frame from the demo video Apple left in macOS 26.7, alongside a closer look at the bud. The stem is thicker than the AirPods Pro 3. (Image: MacRumors/Aaron Perris)

Apple employees have been wearing prototypes for months

A September launch could be on the table, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro

The first real look at Apple's camera AirPods didn't come from the usual suspects. It came from Apple, by mistake. Buried in the macOS Tahoe 26.7 release candidate that landed Monday is a short demo video showing a man wearing AirPods holding up a book, with a Siri voiceover explaining that Visual Intelligence makes "your world becomes savable" and that you can ask it to save what you're looking at for later. MacRumors found the clip.You have to look twice to spot what's different. The bud in the video could pass for an AirPods Pro 3. No visible lens, no sensor housing, just a stem that reads slightly thicker than the current one. MacRumors also found the release candidate littered with references to codename B790, including an error string about an image stream failing on the left bud. Elsewhere in the same build: a warning telling users to keep the AirPods uncovered so the system can read their surroundings accurately. Long hair, evidently, is a known problem.What the cameras actually do is narrower than it sounds. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, they capture low-resolution visual information for Siri to reason about, not photos or video. Look at what's in your fridge, ask what to cook. Walk somewhere and get directions that account for what's in front of you.The demo fits that description. Nobody takes a picture in it. A man looks at a book, Siri saves the book, and that is the whole feature.Gurman has also described longer stems and an LED that lights up when visual data goes to the cloud. Neither turns up in the video.Apple testers have been using prototypes daily since at least May, Bloomberg reported at the time, at the design validation test stage. That is the step immediately before production validation, which means the physical design is locked and what follows is a manufacturing problem rather than a product one. Everything after DVT is about yields and tooling. It also explains why the software looks finished. A team that far along has hardware stable enough to build onboarding screens against, which is exactly what turned up in macOS this week.Earlier this month, Bloomberg reported that camera AirPods could arrive as soon as this year, pulling forward a device most people had penciled in for 2027. Apple's iPhone event is expected in early September, where the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max and the first foldable iPhone are due.One wrinkle worth keeping straight: B790 is not the camera AirPods Gurman has been writing about since 2025. That model, B798, slipped to 2027 after Apple's Siri delays. B790 is a separate project that got there first.Apple, as usual, hasn't confirmed any of it. But a release candidate is the last build before public release, and this one already has setup screens and error messages for the thing. That normally means the hardware is done. September will tell us the rest.
Article Summary: AirPods cameras are for Siri, not for you to click photos. The bud in the video could pass for an AirPods Pro 3. Apple employees have been wearing prototypes for months. A September launch could be on the table, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro.

Article Title: In 2005 for the first time, scientists documented giant squid in their natural habitat, since then many mysteries about their lives remain in ...
Article Text:
A diorama unlike any other in the museum

The real-life battle behind the display

Decades of mystery, only recently interrupted

An unassuming black box near the American Museum of Natural History's iconic blue whale draws in unsuspecting visitors to one of the museum's most striking exhibits, according to a Popular Science report. Every few seconds, a light flashes inside an otherwise pitch-black display, briefly revealing a row of sharp teeth and reddish tentacles as a sperm whale clamps down on a giant squid. The Sperm Whale and Giant Squid Diorama offers a rare, dramatic glimpse into one of the ocean's most mysterious predator-prey relationships, one that scientists are still working to fully understand.Unlike most of AMNH's other displays, this diorama has no glass front. Instead, its dark, reflective interior creates a mirror-like effect that reportedly confused early visitors into thinking the exhibit was empty. The darkness isn't incidental, it's designed to recreate the lightless conditions of the deep ocean, where sunlight never reaches.That same design also makes the diorama unusually labor-intensive to clean. In a video recently shared on social media, AMNH Exhibition Maintenance staffer Janet Spiller can be seen using a backpack vacuum fitted with fiber pole attachments to reach into the exhibit's nooks and crannies, a job that can take a single person up to four hours to complete.The scene depicted in the diorama reflects a genuine and extreme biological encounter. Sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) are known to dive more than 6,500 feet, a depth equivalent to stacking roughly four and a half Empire State Buildings on top of one another, and can remain submerged for over 60 minutes at a time in pursuit of giant squid (Architeuthis dux).Much of what scientists know about this underwater clash comes from indirect evidence rather than direct observation. Sperm whales are sometimes found with circular marks on their skin, believed to be sucker marks left behind from squid fighting to escape. Researchers have also recovered giant squid beaks, the hard biting structures used by the animal, inside the stomachs of sperm whales, offering further proof of these deep-sea encounters.Despite the drama depicted in exhibits like this one, giant squid remain one of the ocean's most elusive animals. Scientists did not document a giant squid in its natural habitat on camera until 2005, and even now, many aspects of the species' life in the deep ocean remain largely unknown. The persistence of that mystery is part of what continues to make the predator-prey relationship between sperm whales and giant squid such a compelling subject for both researchers and museum visitors alike.
Article Summary: The Sperm Whale and Giant Squid Diorama offers a rare, dramatic glimpse into one of the ocean's most mysterious predator-prey relationships. Unlike most of AMNH's other displays, this diorama has no glass front. Its dark, reflective interior creates a mirror-like effect that reportedly confused early visitors into thinking the exhibit was empty.

Article Title: Quote of the day by Jeff Bezos: “I think frugality drives innovation, just like other constraints do. One of…”
Article Text:
Image: AP News

Quote of the day by Jeff Bezos

“I think frugality drives innovation, just like other constraints do. One of the only ways to get out of a tight box is to invent your way out.”

What does this quote mean?

Limitations can force us to think differently

Necessity has a long history of creating innovation

Frugality can make innovation more efficient

Constraints can turn problems into creative challenges

Creativity often grows outside the comfort zone

Why this quote still matters today

Innovation is often associated with having more, more money, more resources, more advanced technology and more time. But some of the most creative solutions emerge when those advantages are limited. Jeff Bezos captured this idea when he said, “I think frugality drives innovation, just like other constraints do. One of the only ways to get out of a tight box is to invent your way out.” His words suggest that limitations do not always prevent progress. Sometimes, they force people to think differently, question familiar methods and find solutions that would never have emerged in more comfortable circumstances.Jeff Bezos (1964-present) is an American entrepreneur and founder of Amazon. He built the company from an online bookseller into one of the world's largest technology and e-commerce businesses and has also pursued ventures in space exploration through Blue Origin. His observation highlights how constraints can turn necessity into a catalyst for experimentation and inventive thinking.This statement implies that scarcity of resources can be an impetus for innovation. When there are no simple solutions, people are obliged to rethink how to do things. Tight budget, shortage of materials, or technical difficulties can become the grounds for experimenting rather than excuses for inaction. The main message that Bezos tries to convey here is that constraints can make people innovative.In the case of abundance of resources, it is easy to find a solution by adding more resources, people, tools or funds. Constraints take away that luxury. All of a sudden, efficiency becomes the priority, and common assumptions should be questioned. A constrained team might discover a simpler way of doing things just because they do not have enough means to operate according to the traditional way.Useful innovations have often been developed due to people’s needs for solving certain problems using what was already available at hand. In cases ranging from simple farming implements to sophisticated medical gadgets that operate in conditions of limited resources, necessity has proved time and again to breed creativity. In the absence of an apparent solution, people start to search for other ways of solving their problems.Innovation does not necessarily mean that you should develop something that is larger or more complicated than your current product. Some of the most outstanding solutions come when people try to do the same thing using less material resources or reducing superfluous steps in a process. This way, frugality may become another incentive for inventors to find what really matters.It may seem as if a hard constraint makes the issue a roadblock. However, perceiving a limitation as a challenge will make a difference in the mindset when it comes to dealing with an issue. The question from “Why can't we do this?” will turn into “How could we do this differently?” This approach can foster experimenting and coming up with unique ideas.Comfort can help one to carry on with the things as usual. Constraints break up the sense of comfort. They make one think and come up with new options. Regardless of whether one is starting a business, developing a product or even solving a simple problem, constraints can provide a different perspective of creativity than abundance can.Whether it be startups trying to innovate on meager resources or scientists innovating the technology to suit a harsh environment, innovations often emerge when there is a sense of urgency involved. The words of Jeff Bezos provide an excellent point that lack of resources should not necessarily translate into lack of opportunities. In some cases, the very fact that there is no easy way out leads to innovation of a solution. The lesson from the statement is quite straightforward: Innovation occurs when nothing else works.
Article Summary: Jeff Bezos is an American entrepreneur and founder of Amazon. He said, “I think frugality drives innovation, just like other constraints do. One of the only ways to get out of a tight box is to invent your way out” His words suggest that limitations do not always prevent progress.
