Article Title: Tata Play is offering 4 months of Spotify Premium for free: Here's how to claim it
Article Text:
How to claim four months of Spotify Premium through Tata Play

Tata Play Spotify Premium offer : What users get

Tata Play has partnered with Spotify to offer its users four months of Spotify Premium Standard at no additional cost. The offer is available to Tata Play subscribers new to Spotify Premium and includes ad-free music playback, audio quality up to 320kbps, and offline listening. The partnership brings music streaming into Tata Play's existing bouquet of services, which until now have centred largely around live television and OTT video content.The offer is being rolled out in phases, starting with Tata Play Binge subscribers before extending to users of the Tata Play Mobile App. For subscribers who have not previously used Spotify Premium, the offer lets them try the paid tier of the music service without committing to a subscription fee for the initial four-month period, subject to eligibility and redemption terms set by the two companies.To redeem the offer, eligible subscribers need to access a promotional code made available through Tata Play's platforms. Tata Play Binge subscribers can claim the code starting August 17, with the rollout on the Tata Play Mobile App following at a later date.Once the code is redeemed on the Spotify app, users can log into Spotify Premium on supported devices for the four-month period at no extra cost. Once the promotional period ends, the standard terms and pricing for Spotify Premium are expected to kick in, though the company has not specified how the continuation or cancellation process will work.The Spotify Premium Standard plan removes advertisements from playback and supports audio quality of up to 320kbps. It also lets users download tracks, albums, and playlists for offline listening, includes unlimited skips, and provides access to a catalogue of more than 100 million songs and over 7 million podcast titles. The subscription works across compatible devices, so access is not limited to Tata Play's set-top box or app.Tata Play Binge brings together multiple OTT apps under a single interface, letting subscribers browse and access video content from different platforms in one place. The Tata Play Mobile App, separately, is built around live TV viewing on smartphones and other supported devices.With the Spotify tie-up, Tata Play is adding audio streaming to a portfolio built so far around video and television, though the company has not indicated whether it plans further extensions to the partnership once the four-month promotional period concludes.

Article Title: USB4 vs USB-C explained: Speeds, cable lengths and the one spec that nobody reads
Article Text:
USB-C is the plug. USB4 is the standard. Knowing which is which decides what you should pay.

The difference between USB4 and USB-C is simple: one is a shape, the other is a set of rules

Is USB-C the same as USB4? Every USB4 cable is USB-C, but almost no USB-C cable is USB4

How to tell if your laptop has USB4, because the port almost never says so

USB4 vs Thunderbolt 4 comes down to certification, not speed, since both stop at 40Gbps

USB4 cable length is the spec nobody reads and the one that quietly ruins setups

USB4 vs USB-C : Which one to buy, and which one do you really need

There is a drawer in most homes now that holds eight or nine cables with the same oval plug on the end, and no way of telling which one is which. One of them charges a laptop. One transfers at speeds that feel like punishment. One came free with a pair of earbuds and does almost nothing beyond keeping them alive. They are physically identical, they all fit every port in the house, and the only difference between them is invisible.That is the whole USB4 versus USB-C problem in one image. USB-C is the shape. USB4 is what the wires inside are allowed to do. The two words turn up on the same spec sheet constantly, often in the same line, which is why they get treated as versions of each other. They are not. A laptop advertising "USB-C ports" has told you nothing about speed, video output or charging. A laptop advertising USB4 has committed to something specific.USB-C arrived in 2014 as a physical redesign. Twenty-four pins, reversible, small enough for a phone and sturdy enough for a workstation. It solved the flipping problem and nothing else. Speed, video and power delivery were all left to whatever protocol the manufacturer decided to run over those pins, which could be anything from USB 2.0 at 480Mbps upward.USB4 is that protocol. The USB Implementers Forum published it in 2019, built on a Thunderbolt 3 specification Intel donated to the group. The number people quote is 40Gbps, but the more useful change is tunnelling. USB4 carries DisplayPort and PCIe traffic alongside ordinary data, and reallocates bandwidth on the fly depending on whether you are copying a file or pushing pixels to a monitor. That is what makes single-cable docking work at all. One connection to a dock and the laptop picks up displays, storage, ethernet and up to 100W of charging, with the Extended Power Range spec reaching 240W on hardware that supports it.Worth sitting with, because it explains most of the confusion. The relationship runs one way. USB4 requires the USB-C connector, so every USB4 cable ends in one. USB-C requires nothing in return, so the majority of USB-C cables in circulation are running much older standards underneath.The chain runs at the speed of its slowest link, and there are three links. Plug a 40Gbps SSD into a USB 3.2 Gen 2 port and you get 10Gbps. Plug that same SSD into a proper USB4 port using a cable that came free in a phone box, and you may get 480Mbps, because the cable is the bottleneck and nothing on screen will tell you so. Files will still copy. They will just take an amount of time that makes no sense given what you paid for the drive.Naming has not helped. USB 3.0 became USB 3.1 Gen 1, then USB 3.2 Gen 1, three names for identical 5Gbps hardware. The USB-IF's response has been to abandon generation numbers in consumer-facing marketing and push speed logos instead, so packaging now reads "USB 40Gbps" or "USB 80Gbps." That is a real improvement, though it only applies to products certified after the change.On the hardware itself, look for a small USB4 marking beside the port, or a Thunderbolt lightning bolt, since Thunderbolt 4 and 5 ports also carry USB4. Plenty of laptops print nothing at all, in which case the spec sheet is the only honest source. Manufacturers also mix port types on the same machine, so the two ports on the left may run at 40Gbps while the one on the right handles 10Gbps and no video. Checking each port individually is tedious and occasionally necessary.The two are close enough that the distinction is mostly about guarantees. Thunderbolt 4 sets a floor: two 4K displays or one 8K, 32Gbps of PCIe bandwidth for storage, mandatory charging support on at least one port. USB4 makes several of those optional, which means one USB4 laptop can drive dual monitors and an external GPU while another handles a single display and refuses the eGPU entirely. Both are correctly labelled.Above that sits USB4 Version 2.0, ratified in 2022 and now on flagship laptops, which doubles throughput to 80Gbps and can run asymmetrically at 120Gbps in one direction for high-refresh displays. Thunderbolt 5 matches it with stricter certification. Whether any of this registers depends entirely on what you connect. For someone editing 4K footage off an external drive, 40Gbps against 10Gbps is the difference between a short wait and a coffee break. For a wired mouse, a keyboard and a printer, it is theoretical.Passive USB4 cables hold full speed only over short runs, roughly 0.8 metres per the specification, which is why certified ones are conspicuously stubby. Longer passive cables drop to half rate. Active cables carry signal-conditioning chips that maintain throughput over greater distances, but they cost more and are less reliably backward compatible with ordinary USB-C peripherals.Power ratings vary independently of all this. A cable can pass 40Gbps and still refuse to charge a laptop, because the wattage it supports is a separate line on a spec sheet most listings never bother to include. In India, a certified 40Gbps cable from a known brand generally runs between Rs 1,500 and Rs 4,000 against a few hundred rupees for an unmarked one. The cheap cable is not fake so much as unspecified, and unspecified is the problem. If a listing states neither a data rate nor a wattage, assume the worst of both.There is no choosing between them, which is the first thing to settle. Buy a USB4 cable and you get USB-C by definition. The actual decision is whether the USB4 premium buys you anything.If you run a dock, an external SSD, an eGPU or a second monitor off your laptop, it does, and the appeal of USB4 is that you stop having to think about any of this. Compliant devices at both ends will negotiate the fastest speeds they support without intervention, and the cable still charges older USB-C hardware because backward compatibility is built in.If all you do is charge a phone and plug in a mouse, it does not. A dedicated 100W power delivery cable running USB 2.0 sells for Rs 400 to Rs 900 and will charge exactly as fast as the Rs 4,000 one, because charging wattage and data throughput are separate specifications that happen to share a plug. Most people need one good USB4 cable for the desk and cheap PD cables everywhere else. Buying the expensive one four times over is the common mistake, and it costs more than the cable that actually needed replacing.Which brings it back to the drawer. It was never lying. It simply never said anything, and neither did most of the people selling the contents. Sort it once, put tape on the fast ones, and the question stops coming up.
Article Summary: The difference between USB4 and USB-C is simple: one is a shape, the other is a set of rules. Knowing which is which decides what you should pay. The relationship runs one way: USB4 requires the USB- C connector, so every USB4 cable ends in one. USB4 carries DisplayPort and PCIe traffic alongside ordinary data.

Article Title: Apple threat notifications: What is mercenary spyware and how to protect against it
Article Text:
What exactly is Apple's threat notification

What to do if you get Apple threat notification

General security tips for everyone

Apple recently sent notifications to customers who it suspected to have been targeted with spyware in their devices. The tech giant later confirmed to multiple publications that it sent out the notifications on Thursday to users targeted in 110 countries. By sending these alerts, the company reminded users about one of the most sophisticated digital threats currently in existence: mercenary spyware. If you are one of those who got the term “Apple threat notification” flashing on your screen and wondered what it actually means, here's a breakdown of what these alerts are, why they are sent and what you should do if you ever receive one.Apple threat notifications exist for one specific purpose: to warn and assist users who may have been individually targeted by spyware attacks. In this case, it was a notification for mercenary spyware. These operations are far more advanced than regular cybercrime, and attackers behind them pour in exceptional resources to go after a very small, specific group of people and their devices.Apple says that these attacks cost millions of dollars to carry out and often don’t stay active for very long, which actually makes them harder to detect and stop in time.The good news, though, is that the majority of users will never come across this kind of attack in their lifetime.Citing public reporting and research conducted by civil society groups, cybersecurity researchers, and journalists over the years, Apple says that this level of individually targeted, high-cost cyberattacks has typically been linked to state actors, including private firms that build mercenary spyware for governments, such as the NSO Group's well-known Pegasus tool. While only a small number of individuals end up being targeted, usually journalists, activists, politicians, and diplomats, these attacks are happening constantly and across the globe.If you ever receive one of these alerts, Apple provides extra guidance and recommends steps you can take to secure your accounts and devices, including turning on Lockdown Mode. The company also strongly recommends reaching out to expert organisations for help, such as the Digital Security Helpline run by the nonprofit Access Now, which offers round-the-clock emergency security assistance.While most people will never encounter mercenary spyware, it's still worth following some basic cybersecurity habits.The first is to keep your devices updated with the latest software so you're covered by the newest security patches, and protect them with a passcode, Face ID, or Touch ID.The second most important thing to do is to turn on two-factor authentication along with a strong password for your Apple Account, and enable Stolen Device Protection for extra peace of mind.While Apple doesn’t allow installing apps from third-party stores, ensure that you download apps only from the App Store, use strong and unique passwords across your accounts, opt for passkeys wherever they're availableFinally, Avoid clicking on links or opening attachments sent by unknown senders.
Article Summary: Apple recently sent notifications to customers who it suspected to have been targeted with spyware in their devices. The tech giant confirmed to multiple publications that it sent out the notifications on Thursday to users targeted in 110 countries. By sending these alerts, the company reminded users about one of the most sophisticated digital threats currently in existence: mercenary spyware.

Article Title: Fireflies.ai brings its AI notetaker to the inbox with Email Assistant, now free on all plans
Article Text:
Meeting context is the part rival AI email tools can't copy

Fireflies.ai, the AI meeting assistant used by more than 20 million people and teams at 75% of Fortune 500 companies, has moved into the inbox. On Friday the company launched Email Assistant, which plugs into Gmail or Outlook and treats email the way it already treats calls—sorting what lands, labelling it by priority, and dropping drafted replies into the thread before you get to them.The pitch rests on a familiar arithmetic. Microsoft's 2025 Work Trend Index found the average worker receives 117 emails a day, with 40% of people online at 6am already checking mail and nearly a third back at it by 10pm—the "infinite workday" Microsoft has been warning about. Fireflies' argument is simpler than most: if it sat in on the call, it already knows what the reply should say.That is the actual differentiator here. When a prospect or candidate follows up on something discussed weeks ago, Email Assistant pulls from both the thread and past meetings with that person, so users aren't reconstructing the conversation from memory. Auto Labels triages incoming mail without touching existing rules or filters. Auto Draft Replies writes in a tone set through custom Writing Instructions, and nothing sends without review. If a sent email goes quiet, a follow-up is drafted in the same thread after a waiting period you configure. AskFred handles plain-English requests—find an email, summarise a thread, pull this week's action items.Insights from email now also feed the Daily Brief alongside meetings and Slack. Meeting Prep, Tasks and AI Skills will draw on email context in the coming months.Email Assistant is available today across all plans, including the free tier. Pro starts at Rs 955 per seat per month, billed annually. Fireflies says it does not train its models on customer data.
Article Summary: Fireflies.ai's Email Assistant plugs into Gmail or Outlook and treats email the way it already treats calls. It pulls from both the thread and past meetings with that person, so users aren't reconstructing the conversation from memory. Email Assistant is available today across all plans, including the free tier.
